entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Sōami (died 1525-11-22), born Shinsō, was a pivotal Japanese ink painter, garden designer, and connoisseur who served as a dōbōshū (artistic advisor) to the Ashikaga shogunate during the late Muromachi period. His artistic lineage traced back to the influential Ami school, founded by his grandfather Nōami and continued by his father Geiami, making him the last and arguably most celebrated of the "Three Amis." Sōami's work was instrumental in synthesizing Chinese Song and Yuan dynasty landscape painting styles with Japanese aesthetic sensibilities, profoundly shaping the development of suibokuga (ink wash painting) and the cultural landscape of Kyoto.

As a dōbōshū, Sōami was not merely an artist but a multi-faceted cultural arbiter for Shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa and later shoguns. He compiled the *Kundaikan Sayūki*, a comprehensive guide to Chinese art collections, display aesthetics, and tea ceremony utensils, which became a foundational text for Japanese art connoisseurship. His painting repertoire included monumental screens and hanging scrolls, particularly known for his *haboku* (splashed ink) landscapes, exemplified by works like the "Landscape of the Four Seasons" at Daisen-in, Daitoku-ji temple. Beyond painting, Sōami applied his aesthetic principles to garden design, notably contributing to the dry landscape (*kare-sansui*) garden of Daisen-in, integrating visual arts with spatial arrangement.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Sōami's work as a painter, garden designer, and cultural arbiter profoundly shaped Japanese aesthetic standards for centuries, particularly through his *Kundaikan Sayūki* and his synthesis of Chinese and Japanese ink painting styles. His influence can be seen in subsequent art schools and the enduring appreciation for Zen gardens.
